newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Still some sparkle in Nordic markets.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Still some sparkle in Nordic markets.

text.p: Investors seeking refuge from a European bond meltdown may venture into Nordic markets to pick up any remaining spread gains, analysts said on Wednesday.
Bright spots like Denmark and Finland are not shielded from the rate hike fears dogging Bunds, but they can be safer, alongside Sweden which has no rate rises on the horizon.
"Denmark is my favourite market now. In terms of relative value versus Germany, the spread is very attractive," said Beshara Madi, senior economist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in London.
Those Nordic currencies likely to stay outside the scope of a European single currency have strongly outperformed against the ailing mark recently, giving their bond markets an edge against Bunds.
In Denmark, a benign inflation outlook and an expected public surplus this year should also put bonds on a strong footing, analysts said.

But given their relative iliquidity, they could be hit harder initially from any possible Bundesbank action to pull the mark back from a slippery slope, which has seen it plunge almost to an eight year low of 1.89 to the dollar.

The Danish central bank would likely follow a Buba action to dampen its own domestic growth, but Madi said over the next three months the 10-year yield spread to Bunds was still forecast at 30-40 basis points from 57 now.
Denmark's May current account surplus on Wednesday was disappointing, and the spread to Bunds had widened from around 47 basis points in the past few days, but Madi said prospects remained bright.
Other analysts meanwhile recommended the long end of Sweden, which they said was underpinned by a strong crown and by the fact that a monetary easing phase had ended.
"It could outperform Italy and Spain. It's outside the EMU uncertainties and fundamentals are very good," said Stephanie Pfeifer, European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
But the short end could be vulnerable to any strength in GDP, analysts said.
Morgan Stanley's Madi was less optimistic on Sweden.

"Sweden is one market where I'm approaching with mixed emotions," he said. "We may have some more upside, but I'm sceptical on the 10-year spread. Given the fundamentals and the attitude to EMU I would be hard pushed to argue for a tighter spread."
The 10-year Swedish spread to Germany was 86 basis points from around 150 in April.
Another potential snag for Sweden was the general election in autumn 1998 which could put pressure on government spending measures.
Finland was also a favoured choice, although most of the convergence has already been achieved with the 10-year spread to Germany now hovering around 25 basis points.

But analysts said Norway looked exhausted on spreads, with robust growth and inflation risks suggesting Norges Bank, the Norwegian central bank, would not hesitate to tighten monetary reins at every opportunity, and irrespective of a German rate rise.
"The only thing that's protecting Norway is that there is no issuance, so I can't be too negative on Norway, but I'm certainly not positive," said Madi.
But some analysts said Nordic bonds looked expensive as they were also vulnerable to an upset in U.S. Treasuries.
"I'm not so sure if I would recommend buying here," said Peter Lindquist, manager Nordic research at HSBC Markets in Stockholm.
But he said the long end of the Swedish curve still offered some potential.
